author: Gregory Thaumaturgus
occasion: Gregory offers a paraphrase of Ecclesiastes, presenting Solomon's teaching on the vanity of human affairs for the benefit of the Church.
argument: Gregory opens by invoking Solomon, son of King David, as the most honored king and wisest prophet, addressing the whole Church of God. He declares that all human affairs and pursuits are empty and useless, because people are defeated by temporal things and wish to look at nothing above the stars with the noble eye of the soul. Human life wears away day by day, like torrents pouring into the boundless deep. What God has established for human life remains fixed, but human words and deeds have no measure, and endless talk brings no profit. Nothing new ever happens; what seems new was already known to the ancients, and both past and present fade into oblivion. Gregory adds that he does not improvise these things as he addresses the Church, but has given them sufficient thought, entrusted as he was with the kingdom of the Hebrews in Jerusalem.

outline.move: Gregory invokes Solomon's authority, declares all human affairs empty, describes the fixed order of creation and the endless, profitless chatter of humanity, affirms that nothing new ever occurs, and notes his own careful reflection as one entrusted with the kingdom of the Hebrews in Jerusalem.

Earnest pursuits or endeavors of human beings.
The Church of God, the community addressed by Gregory.
Idle, wandering talk that brings no benefit.
The human race, characterized as insatiable in speaking and listening.
The passing of winter torrents, an image for the fleeting course of human life.
The noble eye of the soul, capable of seeing above the stars, which humans refuse to use.

scripture: The work paraphrases Ecclesiastes. Use Septuagint book names and numbering; cite as Ecclesiastes (LXX).
uncertain: The precise date of composition is uncertain; the range c. 240–270 AD is inferred from Gregory's lifetime.
Whether the paraphrase was originally composed in Greek or translated from a Syriac original is not established from this source.
